questions.prompt: An origin sends `Cache-Control: no-cache` on its HTML pages. What does a cache that follows RFC 9111 do with them?
choices: It never stores them
It stores them, but sends a conditional request to the origin before every reuse and serves the stored body on a 304
It stores them and reuses them for a default lifetime
Only browsers may store them; shared caches must not
questions.explanation: no-cache means store but revalidate before each use; with an ETag that costs one 304 per request instead of a full download. Keeping a response out of every cache is no-store. nginx is the exception you will meet: it treats no-cache as do-not-store.

questions.prompt: minicache answers a request with `X-Cache-Status: REVALIDATED` and `Cache-Status: minicache; fwd=stale; fwd-status=304; ttl=60`. What happened?
choices: The origin was down and stale-if-error allowed the old copy
The origin sent a new 200 that replaced the stored copy
The copy was fresh and served without contacting the origin

The stored copy was stale; minicache sent If-None-Match with its ETag, the origin answered 304, the 304's headers were merged into the copy and the stored body was served with a fresh 60-second lifetime
questions.explanation: fwd=stale says why the request went to the origin, fwd-status=304 what came back. A new 200 would be EXPIRED with stored, a fresh copy HIT with no fwd, and stale-if-error STALE with detail="stale-if-error".

questions.prompt: Product pages carry `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` and `Vary: Accept-Encoding, User-Agent`. The CDN's hit ratio for them is 3%. Why?
choices: Every distinct User-Agent string is its own variant, so almost every request is a vary-miss even though the page is the same for all of them
public is ignored when Vary is present
Accept-Encoding cannot be used in Vary
Vary disables caching in CDNs
questions.explanation: The secondary key stores the request's User-Agent value with each copy, and there are thousands of distinct values. Drop User-Agent from Vary, or vary on a small normalised header (such as a device class) that the edge computes.

questions.prompt: A response with `max-age=60`, `Date: 09:59:30` and no `Age` header reaches a cache at 10:00:00 (the request took no measurable time). At 10:00:40 another request asks for it. What does the cache do?
choices: Serves it as a hit with Age: 40
Serves it as a hit with Age: 70, because Age matters only to browsers
Treats it as stale: its current age is 70 seconds because the 30 seconds between Date and arrival count as apparent age, so it revalidates
Refuses to store such a response, because Date must equal the arrival time
questions.explanation: RFC 9111 computes apparent_age = response_time - Date = 30, then adds the 40 seconds of resident time. A skewed origin clock therefore makes responses look older, never younger: the formula prefers revalidating early to serving something too old.

questions.prompt: nginx caches a page sent with `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-if-error=600`. It has expired and the single upstream now answers 503. `proxy_cache_use_stale` is not set. What does the client get?
choices: The stale copy, because stale-if-error=600 allows it
A 504 that nginx generates itself
The origin's 503: nginx applies the header's stale-if-error to connection errors and timeouts only, and serving stale on a 503 needs proxy_cache_use_stale http_503
An empty 200
questions.explanation: In ngx_http_upstream.c the header's error window is checked in the path for failed connections, while upstream status codes go through a check of proxy_cache_use_stale alone. minicache, following RFC 5861, serves the stale copy in both cases; the smoke test shows the difference on a running nginx.

questions.prompt: Thousands of clients request the home page in the second its cached copy expires, and the origin falls over. Which change at the cache keeps the origin at one request?
choices: Vary: Cookie, so each client gets its own copy
A longer max-age alone
Cache-Control: no-cache on the home page
stale-while-revalidate on the response, so one background refresh runs while everyone gets the stale copy, plus request collapsing (proxy_cache_lock) for true misses
questions.explanation: A longer max-age only moves the stampede; no-cache and Vary: Cookie send even more traffic to the origin. Serving stale while one refresh runs removes the expiry stampede, and collapsing removes the cold-miss one, as long as the response is storable.
